node-1.label: A 47-year-old woman presented for evaluation of a cardiac murmur without displaying any cardiac symptoms

node-2.label: Heart murmur had been detected at age 3; she had no daily physical restriction except in physical education class, gave birth to two children at ages 26 and 27 without complications, and had no family history of cardiac conditions

node-3.label: The patient noticed her fingers and shoe size getting bigger in her early 30s and experienced menopause at 35 years of age; thickening of all fingers, lips, and nose was observed

node-4.label: Physical examination: height 154.6 cm, weight 63.3 kg (BMI 26.5 kg/m²), blood pressure 106/56 mm Hg, heart rate 68 beats/min, cardiac exam revealed a 4/6 systolic ejection murmur at the second to third left sternal border

why.why: Echocardiography analyzed by the radiologist demonstrates a quadricuspid aortic valve (four equal cusps, spherical morphology) causing severe outflow obstruction with peak gradient 131.1 mm Hg, plus severe LVH and apical aneurysm. This directly confirms a congenital structural lesion and explains the murmur since age 3, benign course, and loud left sternal border systolic ejection murmur. Confidence is increased from 0.55 to 0.95.

Acromegaly features (acral enlargement, early menopause) and severe LVH on echocardiography suggest acromegaly may contribute to hypertrophy, but the radiologist's finding of a quadricuspid aortic valve causing severe outflow obstruction establishes a congenital structural lesion as the primary cause. The murmur since age 3 also predates acromegalic features. Therefore acromegaly is at most a secondary modifying condition, and confidence is reduced from 0.35 to 0.2.

Echocardiography reveals an organic quadricuspid aortic valve with severe outflow obstruction (peak gradient 131.1 mm Hg), which is incompatible with an innocent/functional murmur. The loud 4/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left sternal border and murmur since age 3 further support an organic lesion. Confidence is reduced from 0.1 to 0.01.

The radiologist's analysis confirms congenital heart disease as the primary diagnosis.

attrs.why: Echocardiography demonstrates severe outflow obstruction with peak gradient 131.1 mm Hg together with severe left ventricular hypertrophy and an apical aneurysm. In the setting of a congenital quadricuspid aortic valve, the apical aneurysm is best explained as a complication of chronic pressure overload and hypertrophy, consistent with the radiologist's interpretation that the congenital valve lesion is primary.
